analysis.title: GS Basics - Stocks Up/Momentum Down. Vol Crush. Min Vol Breakout
key_insights: Equities bought the post-midterm dip, led by everything not tied to semiconductors. Two takeaways from the midterms: anti-AI regulation will likely slow CapEx, and the Iran war's unpopularity has eroded the oil risk premium as markets price an earlier end to the conflict.
Asia reflected the rotation: onshore China was bid, Nifty rose 2% on lower oil, and KOSPI fell 5% with Hynix and the AI complex catching down to the US.

Index vol fell sharply. VIX dropped 20% to 16.61 and VXN dropped 18% to 25.08. Hyperscalers led, with a quality bid and defensives and consumer participating. The author calls it rotation, not wholesale liquidation, and says the next move is more complicated now that macro uncertainty is receding and nets are low with hedges in place.

The author says he got AI wrong. Tech flows in Europe were overwhelmingly bearish, with long-only and hedge funds selling chips through infrastructure. Multiples have compressed and positioning was already derisked before another wave of selling. Some moves looked capitulatory.

The market is pricing peak CapEx growth. The author does not think it must also price an outright spending decline: delayed projects are not cancelled demand, but they could create an inventory glut across chips, turbines, cooling and electrical equipment. The risk is an inventory cycle, not demand destruction, and it could weigh on semiconductor capacity expansion at ASML and TSMC.

Existing energised compute becomes more valuable. Hyperscalers may earn better economics on scarce capacity, and constrained expansion means less CapEx and higher FCF. Amazon rallied hard despite last week's FCF concerns. Scarcity favours owners of capacity and hurts those whose valuations depend on building it.

Physical Brent traded at a $2.87 discount to Dated Brent yesterday, reportedly a record extreme, versus a premium above $20/bl three weeks ago. November CFDs and the front three weeks of Dated Brent are in contango. Prompt Brent fell about $8.50 to roughly $94. Some argue fair value is below $70. The author warns of weekend escalation risk.

Gold is framed as an inverse oil trade. EM central banks that hold gold as reserves had to sell or stop buying when energy bills rose, and as oil falls the funding pressure eases and gold catches a bid. The author calls this unproven but more compelling than real rates alone, and says long gold may be a more defensible de-escalation trade than short oil given how much premium has already come out.

Market reversed when Trump signalled willingness to work with Democrats. The author reads the blue sweep as bringing tougher data center regulation but not a binary moratorium, and sees betting markets shifting to more moderate 2028 candidates.

Breadth is improving while the most crowded growth trade unwinds. Transports, aerospace and consumer are showing optimism as oil falls. The author thinks nets are too low for the broader market to fall easily and expects vol compression, stable rates and lower oil to support a grind higher, with AI in the backseat.

tension_points.bull_case: Delayed projects are not cancelled demand, multiples have compressed, positioning was derisked and some selling looked capitulatory. Existing energised compute gains value, with higher FCF for hyperscalers.

tension_points.what_invalidates: Tougher data center regulation turning into a binary moratorium, rather than the more moderate outcome the author expects.
